routes.label: Double and track the jump number

question: The Incredible Hulk can double the distance he jumps with each succeeding jump. If his first jump is \(1\) meter, the second jump is \(2\) meters, the third jump is \(4\) meters, and so on, then on which jump will he first be able to jump more than \(1\) kilometer?
solution:
One kilometer is \(1000\) meters, so we need the first jump whose distance exceeds \(1000\) meters. Starting with the first jump, repeatedly double the distance. The distances in meters are
\[
\begin{aligned}
&1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 8,\ 16,\ 32,\\
&64,\ 128,\ 256,\ 512,\ 1024.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are the first through eleventh jumps, respectively. The tenth jump is \(512\) meters, and every earlier jump is shorter. The eleventh jump is \(1024>1000\) meters, so it is the first to exceed one kilometer. The answer is the \(11\)th jump, choice C.

edges.reason: A recurrence expresses a later term through earlier ones. That only makes sense once a sequence is understood as an ordered list with definite positions, so computing terms step by step depends on it.
edges.scope: ordered terms referenced by previous and next index

edges.reason: The closed form a1*q^(n-1) is one compact route. Repeatedly multiplying the current amount by the fixed factor computes a permitted finite future quantity without forming or evaluating that general-term formula. Claude identifies the same resulting sequence value but does not establish necessity of the particular procedure; retain the named method component.
edges.scope: Using the explicit geometric general-term formula for a future fixed-rate quantity

edges.reason: Counting how many and reading an ordinal position both use the ordered counting sequence one through five.
A kilometer is defined as one thousand meters, so meter meaning is directly present in this conversion relation.

Written addition prepares vertical alignment and repeated carrying. In multiplication the carried amount is added to one digit product, so the full three-digit column-addition procedure is not executed.

The general digit-by-digit multiplication algorithm contains digit products with seven, eight and nine. Their values are required, without demanding rote recitation as the exclusive way to obtain them.
